2. Brief facts, as per prosecution version, as has been culled out from the impugned order that may be taken note of:

4. Arguments were advanced by either side.

5. It was submitted by the ld. counsel for the revisionist that the present FIR registered on the complaint of the respondent no. 2 is based on false and concocted story with the sole intention to harass the revisionist.

It was submitted that the allegations against the revisionist i.e. of forging of birth certificate of her daughter has no basis since she had pointed out to the IO, during investigations that the same was supplied by her husband only and for the same, the CCTV footages of the Ambience Mall, Vasant Kunj for 30.06.2023 can be seen, but the same was never undertaken by the IO.
It was submitted that the impugned order whereby the revisionist has been charged for commission of the offence u/s 420/466/468/471 IPC is bad in law.

It was submitted that there are matrimonial disputes between the parties i.e. the revisionist and the complainant and the ld. Trial Court erred in Crl Rev No. 446/2025 Mithila Murada vs. State of NCT of Delhi & Anr Page No. 2 of 10 observing that the proceedings are nothing but to settle personal scores.

sentences.text: 7. Considered.
Records perused.

8. The present revision petition challenges the order dated 05.06.2025 passed by the learned Trial Court whereby charges were framed against the petitioner under Sections 420/471/465/466 of the IPC in Crl Rev No. 446/2025 Mithila Murada vs. State of NCT of Delhi & Anr Page No. 4 of 10 connection with submission of a birth certificate during the passport application process of her minor child.

entities.text: Crl Rev No. 446/2025 Mithila Murada vs. State of NCT of Delhi & Anr
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 9. The case of the prosecution, in substance, is that the petitioner submitted a birth certificate with the passport authority which the Municipal Corporation, Gurugram, Haryana denied having issued by it.
On this basis, offences of forgery, using forged document as genuine and cheating are alleged against her.
10.It is not in dispute that the passport was not issued on the basis of the disputed birth certificate.
Upon verification by the passport authority, the verified birth certificate was furnished and only thereafter was the passport granted.
It is also borne out from the record that despite being apprised of the alleged discrepancy, the passport authority neither initiated penal proceedings nor lodged any complaint.
The matter arises in the backdrop of matrimonial discord between the petitioner and her husband.

Mithila Muratla vs State on 28 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/142560206/
3 11.At the stage of framing charge, the Court is required to determine whether the material placed on record, taken at face value, discloses the essential ingredients of the alleged offences and raises grave suspicion against the accused.

entities.text:
Mithila Muratla vs State on 28 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/142560206/
3
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
While a meticulous appreciation of evidence is impermissible,
the existence of foundational facts constituting the offence is indispensable.
Suspicion, however strong, cannot substitute statutory ingredients of the offence.
12.It was argued by Ld.Counsel for the respondent that whether the certificate is forged is a question of fact , which can only be proved after trial and therefore discharge is impermissible.

While disputed factual issues ordinarily fall within the domain of trial, the Court must Crl Rev No.
446/2025 Mithila Murada vs. State of NCT of Delhi & Anr Page No. 5 of 10 first ascertain whether the prosecution material itself discloses the essential ingredients of the offence.

entities.text:
Crl Rev No.
446/2025 Mithila Murada vs. State of NCT of Delhi
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Where there is no material connecting the accused with the making of the alleged forged document, directing him to face trial would amount to subjecting him to a roving enquiry unsupported by foundational facts.
Discharge is warranted where the ingredients of the offence are absent on the face of the record.
13.Now, insofar as the charges under Sections 465 and 466 IPC are concerned, the sine qua non for both offences is the making of a false document within the meaning of Section 464 IPC.
The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Sheila Sebastian v. R. Jawaharaj (Supra) has categorically held that to constitute forgery, the accused must have made the false document.
A person who is not the maker of the document cannot be prosecuted for forgery merely because the document is false.
In the present case, the prosecution material merely reflects that the issuing authority i.e the Municipal Corporation , Gurugram denied issuance of the birth certificate.
There is no material whatsoever demonstrating that the petitioner fabricated, altered, procured fabrication of, or participated in the making of the alleged forged document.
No forensic opinion, handwriting comparison, digital recovery, or witness testimony connects the petitioner with the act of fabrication.
The act of filling the passport application using particulars contained in the disputed certificate does not amount to making a false document.
In absence of any material linking the petitioner to the making of the document, the essential ingredient of forgery is not disclosed.
Consequently, charges under Sections 465 Crl Rev No. 446/2025 Mithila Murada vs. State of NCT of Delhi & Anr Page No. 6 of 10 and 466 IPC are unsustainable.

entities.text: Crl Rev No. 446/2025 Mithila Murada vs. State of NCT of Delhi & Anr Page No. 6 of 10 and 466
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 14.With regard to Section 420 IPC, the offence of cheating requires deception, dishonest inducement, and delivery of property or resulting wrongful gain or loss.

In the present case,
admittedly the passport was not issued on the basis of the disputed certificate.
The verified birth certificate was taken, and only thereafter was the passport granted.
No property was delivered, nor did any wrongful gain accrue, nor any wrongful loss occur on account of the alleged forged document.

In Mariam Fasihuddin v. State by Adugodi Police Station (Supra), the Hon'ble Supreme Court emphasized that in absence of wrongful gain or wrongful loss and dishonest inducement, the offence of cheating is not made out.

entities.text: Mariam Fasihuddin v. State by Adugodi Police Station
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Applying that principle to the present case, the ingredients of Section 420 IPC are conspicuously absent, more so when there is no complaint from either the Passport Authority or the Municipal Corporation , Gurugram.

15.As regards Section 471 IPC, the prosecution must establish not merely use of a forged document,
but its use with knowledge or reason to believe that the document is forged.

Ld. Counsel for the Mithila Muratla vs State on 28 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/142560206/
4

entities.text: Mithila Muratla vs State on 28 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: respondent had vehemently argued that the petitioner filled the passport application using particulars from the disputed certificate.
However, the material on record does not disclose circumstances from which knowledge or reason to believe that the document was forged can reasonably be inferred.

The petitioner has asserted that the certificate was handed over to her by her husband, and it is borne out that she also moved an application seeking preservation of CCTV footage of the alleged place of handing over.
Such conduct is not prima facie Crl Rev No. 446/2025 Mithila Murada vs. State of NCT of Delhi & Anr Page No. 7 of 10 indicative of guilty intent.

entities.text: Crl Rev No. 446/2025 Mithila Murada vs. State of NCT of Delhi & Anr
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Counsel for the respondent No. 2 while referring the charge sheet had also contended that notices under Sections 91 and 41A CrPC were issued calling upon the petitioner to produce her laptop and mobile devices for the purpose of investigation and that she did not comply.
17.Non-production of electronic devices cannot substitute the prosecution's obligation to establish foundational facts constituting the offence.
The investigating agency was not precluded from seeking appropriate coercive measures in accordance with law, including search or seizure, yet no such steps were undertaken.
In absence of any material recovered linking the petitioner to fabrication or conscious knowledge, adverse inference cannot be drawn at the stage of framing charge.

18.Significantly, the passport authority, despite being informed/aware of the alleged discrepancy,
did not initiate penal proceedings and did not act upon the disputed certificate.
Instead, only on the basis of the verified birth certificate ,granted the passport lawfully.

Counsel for the respondent No.2 further sought to invoke Section 106 of the Indian Evidence Act, contending that the petitioner alone can explain how she came into possession of the disputed certificate.
I do not concur with the same .
Section 106 of the IEA does not relieve the prosecution of its primary burden to establish the essential ingredients of the offence.
It applies only where foundational facts have been proved and a specific fact lies exclusively within the knowledge of the accused.

In the present case, the prosecution has not established foundational facts linking the petitioner to fabrication or Crl Rev No. 446/2025 Mithila Murada vs. State of NCT of Delhi & Anr Page No. 8 of 10 demonstrating circumstances indicative of conscious knowledge.

entities.text: Crl Rev No. 446/2025 Mithila Murada vs. State of NCT of Delhi & Anr
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The burden to prove making of a false document or existence of mens rea cannot be shifted to the petitioner under the guise of Section 106 IEA.
The provision cannot be used to cure deficiencies in investigation or to reverse the settled principle that the prosecution must stand on its own legs.
20.The disputed document was neither relied upon nor resulted in any benefit to the petitioner.

In Jupally Lakshmikantha Reddy v. State of Telangana (Supra), the Hon'ble Supreme Court observed that where an allegedly forged document was not required or relied upon for the final outcome and no material advantage accrued, criminal prosecution cannot be sustained in absence of clear mens rea.

entities.text: Jupally Lakshmikantha Reddy v. State of Telangana
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The facts of the present case stand on similar footing.
21.Most importantly, neither the Municipal Authority nor the Passport Issuing Authority has lodged any complaint alleging that they were deceived or induced.

entities.text: Mithila Muratla vs State on 28 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is of considerable significance that the passport ultimately issued was not issued on the strength of the disputed certificate.
For the ultimate issuance of the passport, the verified birth certificate was taken and acted upon.
Thus, no benefit accrued to the revisionist on the basis of the impugned document and no wrongful loss has been demonstrated.
22.Lastly , it also cannot be ignored that the proceedings arise in the Crl Rev No. 446/2025 Mithila Murada vs. State of NCT of Delhi & Anr Page No. 9 of 10 backdrop of matrimonial discord.

entities.text: Crl Rev No. 446/2025 Mithila Murada vs. State of NCT of Delhi & Anr
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Criminal law cannot be permitted to become a means to settle personal scores in matrimonial disputes.

Where foundational ingredients of the alleged offences are absent and institutional authorities,
herein the Passport Authority and Municipal Corporation, Gurugram have not perceived any criminality warranting prosecution, continuation of proceedings risks converting criminal process into a tool of harassment, contrary to the caution expressed in Mariam Fasihuddin (Supra).
23.Thus ,upon careful consideration of the entire material placed on record, this Court finds that even if the prosecution case is accepted at face value, there is no material showing that the petitioner made the alleged forged document, no wrongful gain or loss or dishonest inducement is disclosed,
and no material from which knowledge or reason to believe that the document was forged can be prima facie inferred.
Continuation of criminal proceedings in such circumstances would amount to abuse of the process of law and would subject the petitioner to unwarranted trial in absence of foundational material.
24. Accordingly, the revision petition stands allowed.
The impugned order dated 05.06.2025 for framing charges qua the revisionist/petitioner under Sections 420/471/465/466 IPC is set aside.
The petitioner is discharged of all the aforesaid offences.
